# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why3: This is my own commitment step and my own customers, so I can judge from what I know of them and our 15-day returns whether I hold this belief and whether the bar is fair.
screens.why4: The bar is clear and its escape is fine, but it counts only probably not and no against the belief, so unsure people let "most would order" hold on a $599 purchase.
screens.why5: "Order a pair with free returns" is my step, but the sentence drops the word glasses and the price, and "most ... now" stretches it to every deaf and hard-of-hearing adult rather than those who hit the problem weekly.
screens.instead: Most deaf and hard-of-hearing adults who lost track of a conversation with hearing people this week would order a pair of AirCaps glasses at $599 with free returns now. Holds if no more than 1 in 3 say probably not or no.

screens.why1: I have just named the first real step and am about to send the study, so it makes sense to decide now whether to ask people to take it.
screens.why2: I can answer on first read and the hint explains the mechanics, but "pilot" is a B2B word I wouldn't use for a consumer pair of glasses, where I'd say "try a pair", and I haven't seen the Pilot tab yet.
screens.why3: Whether I want to collect the emails of people ready to try the glasses is entirely my own decision, and I can make it right away.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers the whole choice, the two options are distinct and clear, and no escape chip is needed for a decision that is mine.
screens.why5: My step was "order a pair with free returns", but the line people see shrinks it to a generic "try this for real" and an email, which is a lighter ask than an order and never mentions the glasses or the returns.
screens.instead: Ask people who say yes to order a pair with free returns? The line at the end: "Would you order a pair of AirCaps with free returns? Leave your email." Options: Yes, ask them / No, don't ask

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, choosing who fronts the questions is an obvious last setup step, and the hint settling that typing and tapping work too is what I need to hear for this audience.
screens.why2: The question and the read-or-type reassurance are plain, but 'Keel records the voice you pick' sits oddly beside a choice of who appears on video, and the 'Hear' preview leaves me unsure whether I am picking a face, a voice or both, and '400 credits' needs a second read.
screens.why3: I can decide on cost and fit, but a 5-second audio sample tells me little as a founder whose respondents are largely deaf, because what matters to them is whether the face is lipreadable and the on-screen text is clear, which I can only guess at from this.
screens.why4: Two named interviewers are distinct and enough to pick from, but they are offered only as sound clips, with no look at the face or the captions, which is the part my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents would actually use.
screens.why5: My audience is named in my own words and nothing about my product or its meaning has shifted.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Each question appears on video and in writing, and people can type or tap instead of talking. Options: Daphne (see her ask a question with captions, 5 s) / Saskia (see her ask a question with captions, 5 s).

screens.why1: Choosing how people answer belongs just before sending, but it comes straight after 'who should ask' and partly covers the same ground, since picking Daphne or not is the same choice again.
screens.why2: I understand the choice, but 'Still recording · ready in a few minutes' and 'Ready when Daphne is' need a second read, because it isn't clear that Daphne's video is what's being recorded or that I can wait for it.
screens.why3: I know my people and how they read, talk and use phones, so I can pick the right format from what I know; that's why I chose read and tap.
screens.why4: My true answer is there and the three options are distinct, but the Daphne option sells 'aloud', 'Hear her' and how well she catches speech in loud rooms to deaf people, without saying how she handles deaf speech or whether her video is captioned or signed.
screens.why5: My group is named exactly as I typed it, and nothing here changes what I said about AirCaps or who it is for.
screens.instead: How should deaf and hard-of-hearing adults answer? Read and tap (every question written, answers tapped or typed; ready now) / Daphne on video (every question also written on screen; answer by talking, typing or tapping; spoken answers may be caught less well from deaf voices; her video is still recording, ready in a few minutes) / Let them choose (they pick when they open the link; ready once her video is).

screens.why1: I have just chosen how people answer, so the last thing before sending is deciding who gets the link, and it is obvious why it is asked here.
screens.why2: Named people, a list I found, or one open link in a group are plain to me on first reading, and the only product word, the Contacts page, is explained by the option around it.
screens.why3: I know who I can reach, from the people on our waitlist to the deaf and hard-of-hearing groups where they already gather, so I can answer this from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The three options cover the ways I would really reach people, they are distinct, each says what happens next, and no escape chip is needed for a choice this complete.
screens.why5: The screen changes nothing I typed about the deaf and hard-of-hearing adults I am studying, and my pick of people I know by name is kept as chosen.

screens.why1: As the first question of a study about my life, it makes sense to check straight away whether I regularly talk with hearing people.
screens.why2: I understand it at once, and hearing people is how I would say it myself.
screens.why3: I know from my own week that I talk with hearing people, as I do whenever I go out or to the theatre.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover the whole question and do not overlap, and a screening question like this needs no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the idea of deaf and hard-of-hearing adults talking with hearing people every week, and it leaks no product or role label to me.
screens.why6: It is short and easy to catch when heard once, but the spoken form leaves out the closing Yes or no, so the choices are not said aloud.

screens.why1: An idea card makes sense in a short study, but it comes straight after one yes-or-no about talking with hearing people, with nothing yet about my last conversation, so it feels a bit sudden.
screens.why2: Captions, glasses, lens and eye contact are all words I use, and I would get it on first reading.
screens.why3: Reading captions while trying to keep eye contact with hearing people is my everyday life, so I can picture it straight away.
screens.why4: The screen is a card to read and shows no options.
screens.why5: It is shown on purpose as an idea, says what it does and marks the eye-contact claim as the builders' belief, with no internal terms reaching me.
screens.why6: The sentences are short and say well, but the lens is mentioned twice and 'the app' twice in a few lines, which is a little more than needed when heard once, and a card spoken aloud is no use to me unless the words are also on screen.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, live captions inside the lens. You wear lightweight glasses that show what the people nearby are saying. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: After the idea card, asking what I lost to missed conversations makes sense, but it jumps straight to a count without saying what kind of conversation or what I mean by missing one.
screens.why2: The words are simple, but 'miss' is unclear to me: I might sit through a whole dinner and catch half of it, so I would have to reread and decide whether that counts as missed.
screens.why3: Missing conversation is my daily life, but nobody counts it across a month, and I often do not know what I missed, so any number would be a guess.
screens.why4: The number box and 'None' and 'I can't recall' fit, but 'I'd rather not say' is an extra escape the guidelines say does not exist and it is a second way out beside 'I can't recall'.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product or the founder's terms reaches me here; it stays on my own conversations and keeps the founder's meaning of conversations too hard to follow.
screens.why6: It is short and one question that says well, but a month's count is hard to hold and answer on one hearing, and the chips on screen differ from the one escape spoken aloud.
screens.instead: Think of the last 7 days: about how many conversations with hearing people could you not follow well enough to join? (a number; None; I can't recall)

screens.why1: Asking what the idea is worth makes sense after the idea card, but I've only answered one question about my missed conversations and the heading says 'What you do today', so it feels abrupt.
screens.why2: I understand the dollar amounts, but 'worth to you up front' needs a second read, and 'inside the lens' doesn't quite tell me I'd be wearing glasses.
screens.why3: I know what missing a conversation costs me and what hearing devices can cost, but I'd be partly guessing at a price for something I've never tried.
screens.why4: The bands are distinct and complete and 'I can't say' fits, but $599 looks oddly specific next to the round numbers and makes me think it's the real price.
screens.why5: The idea stays as live captions in the lens, but the odd $599 edge hints at the company's planned price where I wasn't meant to see it.
screens.why6: Read this way it is two price questions in one breath with six dollar bands each, which I couldn't hold after hearing it once, and the bands aren't split into two steps as the guidelines require.
screens.instead: If AirCaps cost one price up front, what would you pay? Under $250; $250 to under $600; $600 to under $1,000; $1,000 or more; or I wouldn't pay for this. Or say I can't say. Then, on its own: And each month after that? Under $10; $10 to under $20; $20 to under $50; $50 or more; or I wouldn't pay for this. Or say I can't say.

screens.why1: Right after I named a price, it makes obvious sense to ask what would make it worth more to me.
screens.why2: The words are everyday ones and I could answer the first time I read them, without needing a second look.
screens.why3: I know what I struggle to follow in noisy places like the theatre or a restaurant, so I can say what would make captions worth more to me.
screens.why4: It is only a box to type in, with no options to judge.
screens.why5: It names AirCaps, which I was already shown on the idea card, and uses the price I gave, with no founder talk or role labels reaching me.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, but the spoken figures "$250 to under $599" are a bit of a mouthful and "put AirCaps at" is slightly bookish when heard.
screens.instead: You said AirCaps was worth $250 to under $599 to you. What would make it worth more?

screens.why1: After being asked what AirCaps would be worth to me, asking who else had a say in paying makes sense, but it comes abruptly and sounds more like an office purchase than a question about my hearing and conversations.
screens.why2: The words are easy, but I'd have to stop and work out what "something like this" means: captioning glasses, a captioning app or my hearing aids?
screens.why3: If I count hearing aids or a captioning app I can answer from memory, but I've never bought glasses like these, so I'd be guessing at what counts.
screens.why4: "No, someone else decided for me" is odd because someone else did have a say, "several people" overlaps with "someone else", and "I can't recall one" only loosely fits never having bought anything like it.
screens.why5: The product name and founder's terms don't leak here, but "several people had to agree" drifts toward a company sign-off rather than a person with a hearing loss buying for themselves.
screens.why6: It's short with one question and four options I can hold, but the yes and no options aren't in a sensible order, and hearing "No, someone else decided for me" once would make me stop and untangle it.
screens.instead: The last time you paid for a hearing aid or captioning tool, who made the decision? I decided alone; I decided with someone else; or someone else decided for me. Or say I can't recall one.

screens.why1: After the idea and what I'd pay for it, asking whether I'd actually order one is an obvious last question, even if the 'What you do today' label doesn't suit it.
screens.why2: The sentence is short and clear, but 'a pair' of what is left for me to work out from 'lens', because nothing ever says these are glasses.
screens.why3: I know whether I'd try captions in a conversation with hearing people, but with no price on the screen and no word on whether it works with my prescription, my answer is partly a guess.
screens.why4: The options jump from a firm yes to 'Probably not' with no 'Probably yes' to balance them, so a hopeful but unsure person like me has no true answer, and the first option's length doesn't match the others.
screens.why5: The card is shown on purpose and the question only asks about ordering with free returns, so no founder jargon or talk about roles reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question and three options are easy to hold, but said aloud without the card 'a pair' has nothing to refer to and the first option repeats the stem's 'free returns' clause.
screens.instead: If AirCaps glasses were ready today at the price you gave, would you order a pair with free returns, or not? Yes, I would; Probably would; Probably not; or No.
